security-models.hint: First ask what the rule is actually protecting — confidentiality, integrity, or a designated process/relationship — then match the direction (up/down, before/after) to the model that names that exact behavior.

smod-01.label: A junior analyst holding a Confidential clearance tries to open a file stamped Secret; the system blocks the read before the file even opens.
smod-01.why: Blocking a lower-cleared subject from reading a higher-classified object is BLP's confidentiality rule. Biba's simple property runs the opposite direction — it stops reading down, not up — so a scenario about disclosure risk from a lower clearance always points to BLP, not Biba.

smod-02.label: A Secret-cleared officer drafting a briefing is prevented from saving a copy of it into a folder marked Unclassified, even though her own clearance outranks that folder's level.
smod-02.sub: No write down (* / Star Property, confinement)
smod-02.why: Stopping high-classified content from leaking into a lower-classified store is the star property's confinement rule — a confidentiality control. Lattice-based access control is the ordering structure that makes 'higher' and 'lower' meaningful at all, but the actual write-down block is BLP's named rule, not the generic lattice concept.

smod-03.label: Two engineers share the same Secret clearance, but only one of them can open a specific weapons-design file, because only she is listed as needing that file for her project.
smod-03.sub: Discretionary Security Property (need-to-know via access matrix)
smod-03.why: BLP layers a need-to-know access matrix on top of mandatory clearance checks, so two equally-cleared subjects can still be split by discretionary permissions. Brewer-Nash also splits access per-subject, but dynamically, based on prior read history to block a conflict of interest — this is a static need-to-know listing, not a history-driven wall.

smod-04.label: A system configured under its strictest confidentiality mode confines every subject to reading and writing solely within its own classification layer — no reaching up, no reaching down.
smod-04.why: The strong star property is BLP's stricter variant that collapses the simple and star properties into one same-layer-only rule. Biba enforces its own layer restriction for integrity, not confidentiality, so a scenario framed purely around classification layers stays with BLP.

smod-05.label: A production database server running at the highest integrity tier refuses to ingest a data feed pulled from an unvetted, low-integrity staging table.
smod-05.why: Refusing to pull data down from a less-trusted source protects integrity, not confidentiality — Biba's simple property runs opposite BLP's: it blocks reading down, where BLP blocks reading up. A scenario about corrupting trusted data with untrusted input is Biba's territory.

smod-06.label: A contractor account with a low integrity rating is denied write access to the organization's certified configuration-management baseline.
smod-06.why: Preventing a low-integrity subject from writing into a high-integrity object is Biba's star integrity rule — the goal is uncorrupted data, not restricted disclosure. Clark-Wilson also protects integrity, but through a certified transformation procedure rather than a direct label comparison like this one.

smod-07.label: A low-integrity utility script is blocked from calling or invoking a higher-integrity system process at all, even for a read-only status check.
smod-07.why: Barring a lower-integrity subject from invoking a higher-integrity subject at all — not just reading or writing its data — is Biba's invocation property, the model's third integrity rule. That's a different move from Clark-Wilson's approach, which routes changes through a certified program rather than blocking a call outright.

smod-08.label: A manufacturing control system enforces mandatory access purely to stop less-trusted operators from tampering with calibration data, with no rule at all about who is allowed to view the results.
smod-08.why: The named concern is preventing untrusted subjects from corrupting trusted data — integrity, not disclosure — which is what puts this with Biba over BLP. Lattice-based access control is the ordering structure both models sit on, but naming the actual security goal here resolves to a specific model, not the generic lattice concept.

smod-09.label: A bank's funds-transfer application only allows money to move through a fixed, audited sequence of steps; no direct edit to an account balance is ever permitted.
smod-09.why: Forcing every change through a certified, structured procedure instead of a direct edit is Clark-Wilson's well-formed-transaction rule. Biba would simply block a low-integrity subject from writing at all; Clark-Wilson instead lets the write happen, but only through an intermediary program that enforces the correct sequence.

smod-10.label: The clerk who enters a new vendor into the payment system is never the person permitted to approve that vendor's first invoice.
smod-10.why: Splitting a sensitive transaction across two required roles so no single person controls it end to end is Clark-Wilson's separation-of-duties rule, enforced through its subject-program-object triplet. Brewer-Nash also restricts a subject based on prior activity, but to prevent a conflict of interest between competing clients, not to split one transaction between two people.

smod-11.label: Before a new expense-reporting workflow can touch production data, auditors must formally certify it meets the organization's integrity rules, and the platform then refuses to run any workflow that skips that certification step.
smod-11.why: Requiring a program to be certified against integrity rules, then having the system enforce that only certified programs run, is Clark-Wilson's paired certification/enforcement mechanism — a governance process around the transformation procedure itself, not a label comparison the way BLP or Biba operate.

smod-12.label: Payroll records can only be changed by running the approved payroll-adjustment program; no user or script may write to the payroll table directly.
smod-12.sub: Constrained Data Items accessed only through Transformation Procedures
smod-12.why: Routing every change to a protected data item through one designated program is exactly Clark-Wilson's CDI/TP structure. Biba achieves a similar-looking lockdown by comparing integrity labels directly, without requiring a specific intermediary program — the mandatory-program requirement is what marks this as Clark-Wilson.

smod-13.label: An internal-controls team periodically re-runs an independent check confirming the payroll-adjustment program still produces results consistent with the source timesheets it started from.
smod-13.why: An independent audit step that checks a transformation procedure's output for internal and external consistency is Clark-Wilson's Integrity Verification Procedure — a review of the process itself, not a direct read/write permission check the way the other three models operate.

smod-14.label: An investment analyst who has already opened Client A's confidential merger file is automatically blocked from ever opening Client B's file, the moment B is flagged as a competitor in the same deal.
smod-14.why: Access here changes dynamically because of what the subject has already read, to stop one person serving two competing clients — that history-driven wall is Brewer-Nash's signature move. BLP's access matrix is static by comparison: it doesn't lock a door because of what you opened five minutes ago.

smod-15.label: A law firm's document system lets a new associate freely read either of two rival clients' files, but the instant she opens one, the system permanently locks her out of the other.
smod-15.sub: Dynamically changing access based on prior activity
smod-15.why: The rule engages only after the first read and is triggered by a competing-client relationship — a real-time behavioral lockout, not a fixed classification ordering. Lattice-based access control describes an ordering of clearance levels, but there is no clearance hierarchy at play here, just a conflict-of-interest trigger.

smod-16.label: A financial conglomerate's compliance platform is built specifically to stop insider-trading-style leakage between its brokerage and investment-banking arms, based on which accounts each employee has already touched.
smod-16.why: Preventing leakage between competing business units by tracking each employee's own access history is the textbook Brewer-Nash use case. Clark-Wilson's separation of duties splits one transaction across two roles; this instead blocks one person from ever touching two conflicting relationships at all.

smod-17.label: A classification scheme orders every combination of sensitivity level and compartment so that any two labels have one clearly-defined 'least upper bound' a subject would need in order to access both at once.
smod-17.sub: Partially ordered set with defined least-upper-bound / greatest-lower-bound
smod-17.why: Defining a mathematically ordered structure across every label combination, with a computable upper and lower bound for any two labels, is the lattice concept itself — the shared mathematical foundation BLP and Biba are both built on top of. BLP names the specific no-read-up/no-write-down rules that run inside that structure, but this scenario describes the ordering, not one model's read/write rule.

smod-18.label: A defense system assigns every subject and object a label combining a sensitivity tier and a set of compartments, then grants access only when one label's tier and compartment set both dominate the other's.
smod-18.sub: Multilevel security via mandatory, label-based lattice comparison
smod-18.why: Comparing combined tier-plus-compartment labels for dominance is the general lattice-based mandatory-access mechanism underlying multilevel security. Bell-LaPadula is the specific confidentiality policy that runs on top of that structure, but this scenario names the label-comparison mechanism itself, not a no-read-up or no-write-down rule.

smod-19.label: Two departments' security labels each carry different, non-overlapping compartments at the same sensitivity tier; the ordering structure treats them as incomparable, so neither dominates the other and no default access flows either way.
smod-19.sub: Incomparable elements in a partial order (no default flow)
smod-19.why: Incomparability — two labels that are neither greater nor lesser than each other — is a property of the partial-order lattice structure itself, not a rule any single model enforces. Bell-LaPadula only tells you what happens once dominance is established; this scenario is about the ordering rule that decides whether dominance exists at all.
